issues.failure_explanation: For n strictly inside a batch, the proof asserts |a_{n,n}| = sigma_n(f_n) >= sigma_{n~}(f_n) >= sigma_{n~+1}(f_{n~+1}). Only the first element of a batch is chosen by a quality criterion. The other b-1 elements are chosen from the frozen estimator r_{n_}, and the proof states that their choice does not matter. The step sigma_{n~}(f_n) >= sigma_{n~+1}(f_{n~+1}) has no justification. In fact f_n lies in V_{n+1}, which is contained in V_{n~} for n < n~, so sigma_{n~}(f_n) = 0 and the displayed chain is false. The claim itself fails: take X=R^3, F={e1, (cos t, sin t, 0), e2, e3}, b=2, gamma=1. All four elements tie in the estimator ||f||, which the paper allows ('any sequence which can arise'). Pick f_0=e1 and f_1=(cos t, sin t, 0). Then |a_{1,1}| = sin t, which is arbitrarily small, but sigma_{1+b-1}=sigma_2 = dist(e3, V_2) = 1. So gamma*sigma_{n+b-1} <= |a_{n,n}| fails. The same unjustified step is repeated in the Banach version of the lemma.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified. At minimum, either the in-batch selection rule must be changed or restricted so that |a_{n,n}| >= c*gamma*sigma_{n+b-1} can be proved, or the product argument must be redone using only the batch-first elements with a new bookkeeping of the spaces. The constants and the b-dependence would then have to be re-derived.
issues.overall_effect: (P1) is the only place where the batch selection enters the analysis. It feeds the product inequalities in the Hilbert and Banach theorems and all the rates and the loss factor derived from them. With the selection rule as stated (or left arbitrary), no convergence guarantee is established for the batch algorithm.
issues.title: Lower diagonal bound (P1) for non-first batch elements is unsupported and false
issues.why_classification: The key lemma of the paper is false for the algorithm as defined. Repairing it requires either a new selection rule or new proof architecture, and the resulting rates and b-dependence may change materially.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof ends with exponent (n-m)/n, which is the correct one, but the theorem states (n-m)/m. The stated version is not what is proved. It is also false: for m=1 and n large it would give sigma_{n+b-1} <= sqrt2*gamma^{-1} d_1^{n-1}, which is far too strong. It is inconsistent with the 'in particular' sqrt(d_n) statement, which needs exponent 1/2 for n->2n and m=n.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the exponent (n-m)/m by (n-m)/n in the statement, as the proof gives.
issues.overall_effect: Statement (i) of the theorem is wrong as printed, although the proof and the later uses (the sqrt(d_n) corollary and part (iii)) use the correct exponent.
issues.title: Exponent in eq. (wbg_sigman_dn) is (n-m)/m but the proof gives (n-m)/n
issues.why_classification: It is a one-symbol local fix. The proof already supports the corrected statement, and no result or rate changes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: but their values improve ($C_1(n,\hue{b})$ decreases and $c_1(n,\hue{b})$ increases) for increasing $n$, so that the estimates get even sharper.

issues.failure_explanation: The contradiction argument uses one constant C_1 (resp. c_1) in the hypothesis at the indices 2s and s and in the conclusion at M, for all s>=1. Case 1/2 with parameter s then needs C_1 >= 2^{alpha+1} gamma^{-2} ceil(4+(b-1)/s)^{2 alpha} C_0 for every s>=1. This is largest at s=1, giving (b+3)^{2alpha}. Likewise c_1 must be at most the (b+1)-based value for (iii). The constants C_1(n,b), c_1(n,b), which are claimed to improve with n, are not what the argument yields: it is circular to use a smaller n-dependent constant at M while the hypothesis carries a larger one at 2s. The Remark's constants 2*50^alpha*gamma^{-2}*C_0 for n>=b+3 and (1/2)6^{-alpha}c_0 for n>=b+1 additionally drop the second term of the max, resp. the min. Without that term the Case 3 start of the induction (small indices) is not covered unless C_0 is large. So the improvement from the factor (b+3)^{2alpha} to 5^{2alpha} (and 1/(b+1)^alpha to 1/3^alpha) is unproved.

failure_location.quote: Suppose that the statement in (ii) does not hold and let $M$ be the first value where $\sigma_M(\cF)>C_1M^{-\alpha}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the theorem with the uniform constants dominated by the s=1 values. Or give an additional argument, such as restarting the first-failure induction from an index of order b, showing that the improved constants hold for large n with the early indices absorbed.
issues.overall_effect: Only a b-dependent uniform constant of order (b+3)^{2alpha} (resp. (b+1)^{-alpha} in the exponent) is proved. The remarks on asymptotically batch-independent constants, and the (2/3)^alpha loss factor built on them, are unsupported.
issues.title: First-failure argument gives only a uniform constant; n-dependent and improved constants (Remarks) are not established
issues.why_classification: A contained extra argument (or a weaker uniform statement with an explicit b-dependence) repairs it. The theorem and the qualitative rate survive, but the advertised batch-independent constants need a new lemma.

issues.failure_explanation: By the theorem, c_1(n,b) = min{ c_0 2^{-(alpha+1)} ceil(2+(b-1)/n)^{-alpha}, ln(C_1) b^{-alpha} }. The proof sets c_1(n,1) and c_1(n,b) equal to their first branches only. For large c_0 the second branch is the minimum. Then c_1(n,1) = ln C_1 and c_1(n,b) = ln(C_1) b^{-alpha}, so the ratio is b^{-alpha} < (2/3)^alpha for b>=2, not (2/3)^alpha. The corollary identity c_1(n,b) = (2/3)^alpha c_1(n,1) therefore does not follow from the theorem. It is also not a statement about 'asymptotic' rates, because the min term does not disappear as n grows.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the corollary with the minimum retained, or add the hypothesis that the first branch is the smaller one. Alternatively, prove a genuinely asymptotic version and say that the factor (2/3)^alpha applies to the first branch only.
issues.overall_effect: The quantified loss factor (2/3)^alpha, which is used to build the upper bound sigma~(n) in the numerical section, is valid only for c_0 small enough that the first branch of the min is active. In general the proved loss is worse.
issues.title: Corollary on rate loss (2/3)^alpha drops the second branch of the minimum defining c_1
issues.why_classification: The statement must be weakened or conditioned, and the asymptotic claim needs a separate argument. The headline loss factor for general c_0 is lost, but a comparable conditional result survives.

issues.failure_explanation: Case 3 concludes C_1 (4c-1)^{-(alpha-beta-1/2)} >= 1 with c = ceil(2+(b-1)/4). That requires C_1 >= (4c-1)^{alpha-beta-1/2}. The definition of C_1 only contains 4(c-1)^{alpha-beta-1/2} as the second term, which is smaller. For b=1 (c=2) and alpha-beta-1/2 = 1 it gives 4 versus 7. For larger exponents the gap grows (4 versus 7^p). So the contradiction 1 >= ... >= 1 is not obtained for the stated C_1.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the second term in C_1 by (4*ceil(2+(b-1)/4) - 1)^{alpha-beta-1/2}, which is what Case 3 uses. The other cases are unaffected.
issues.overall_effect: The constant C_1(n,b) in part (ii) of the Banach theorem is not shown to give a valid bound for the small indices M < 4c.
issues.title: Banach (ii): second term of C_1 does not dominate the constant needed in Case 3
issues.why_classification: It is a local change of one term in the constant. The method, rate and scope of the result are unchanged.

issues.failure_explanation: For 1<=M<=b the proof claims C_1 sqrt(M) e^{-c_1 M^alpha} >= C_1 sqrt(b) e^{-c_1 b^alpha}. The function M -> sqrt(M) e^{-c_1 M^alpha} is not monotone. For M=1 and small c_1 the left side is about C_1 while the right side is about C_1 sqrt(b), so the inequality fails. What is needed is C_1 sqrt(M) e^{-c_1 M^alpha} >= 1 for all 1<=M<=b. At M=1 this means c_1 <= ln C_1. The theorem only ensures c_1 <= ln(C_1 sqrt(b)) b^{-alpha}, which can exceed ln C_1 when ln C_1 is small. For C_1<1 and c_1>0 the conclusion fails outright.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the second branch of c_1 by a value that guarantees C_1 sqrt(M) e^{-c_1 M^alpha} >= 1 on 1<=M<=b. This can be done by checking the endpoints M=1 and M=b, using concavity in ln M, together with an assumption such as C_1>1.
issues.overall_effect: The start of the first-failure induction (indices M<=b) is not justified, so the claimed bound in (iii) is not proved for the stated c_1(n,b), at least when C_1 is close to or below 1.
issues.title: Banach (iii): Case 3 uses a false monotonicity step for sqrt(M) e^{-c_1 M^alpha}
issues.why_classification: It is a local correction of the constant and of the Case 3 estimate. The structure of the proof and the exponential rate are preserved.
